subject: Psychology
name: Psychology, Units 1 and 2
about: VCE, Development, the brain, social influence and perception
syllabus: VCE Psychology Study Design (from 2023), Units 1 and 2

units.title: Unit 1: How are behaviour and mental processes shaped?

points.title: Nature and nurture together
points.brief: Development comes from heredity (genes passed down) and environment (experiences, people, culture) working together, not from either one alone.

points.title: The biopsychosocial approach
points.brief: A model that explains development and behaviour through biological, psychological and social factors at once, and how they affect each other.

points.title: Emotional development
points.brief: How a person learns to recognise, express and manage emotions, starting with attachment to carers in infancy and growing through childhood and adolescence.

points.title: Cognitive development
points.brief: How thinking, memory and reasoning grow across life, from learning that objects still exist out of sight to reasoning about abstract ideas.

points.title: Social development
points.brief: How relationships, identity and social skills develop across life, from attachment in infancy to forming an identity in adolescence.

points.title: Sensitive and critical periods
points.brief: A sensitive period is a time when a skill develops most easily. A critical period is a narrow window after which some development may not happen at all.

points.title: Criteria for typical behaviour
points.brief: Behaviour can be judged against cultural perspectives, social norms, statistical rarity, personal distress and whether it is maladaptive.

points.title: Limits of each criterion
points.brief: Each criterion has a weakness. Rare behaviour can be healthy, and norms change across cultures and over time, so no single test is enough.

points.title: Neurotypical and neurodivergent
points.brief: Normality and neurotypicality, and whether emotions, behaviours and thoughts are adaptive or maladaptive for a person.

points.title: Neurodiversity
points.brief: Brains develop in many normal ways, so differences such as autism or ADHD are natural variation in the population.

points.title: Who supports mental wellbeing
points.brief: Mental health workers, psychologists, psychiatrists and organisations support development and wellbeing, and diagnose and manage mental health conditions.

chapters.title: How we came to understand the brain

points.title: Brain versus heart debate
points.brief: Early thinkers argued over whether the brain or the heart was the source of thought and feeling. Evidence from injuries and dissection settled it on the brain.

points.title: Mind and body questions
points.brief: Philosophers asked whether the mind is separate from the body (dualism) or part of it (monism). Modern psychology studies mental processes through the brain.

points.title: Phrenology
points.brief: Phrenology claimed bumps on the skull showed a person's traits. It was never supported by evidence, but it pushed the idea that brain areas have different jobs.

points.title: Brain ablation and lesioning
points.brief: Removing or damaging part of an animal's brain and watching what changes showed which areas link to which functions.

points.title: Neuroimaging
points.brief: CT and MRI show the brain's structure. PET and fMRI show which areas are active during a task, so researchers can link function to place.

points.title: Hindbrain, midbrain and forebrain
points.brief: The hindbrain runs survival functions and balance, the midbrain relays sensory and movement information, and the forebrain handles complex thought.

points.title: The cerebellum
points.brief: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and posture, and helps learn motor skills such as riding a bike.

points.title: The cerebral cortex and its lobes
points.brief: The cortex has four lobes: frontal (planning, movement, speech production), parietal (touch and body position), temporal (hearing and memory) and occipital (vision).

points.title: Neuroplasticity
points.brief: The brain changes in response to experience and injury. Learning, exercise, sleep and social contact help keep it working well.

points.title: Acquired brain injury
points.brief: An ABI is damage after birth, from a blow, stroke or lack of oxygen. It can change biological, psychological and social functioning.

points.title: Research on neurological disorders
points.brief: Studies of conditions such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy keep adding to what is known about how the brain works.

points.title: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy
points.brief: CTE is a brain disease linked to repeated head knocks, such as in contact sport. It can affect memory, mood and behaviour, and is confirmed only after death.

points.title: Primary and secondary data in psychology
points.brief: Primary data is collected first-hand; secondary data comes from others' research and must be judged for quality.

points.title: Evidence, opinion and anecdote in psychology
points.brief: Scientific evidence is tested and repeatable. Opinions and personal stories are not, so they cannot settle a question.

points.title: Judging research
points.brief: Good research is valid, comes from an authoritative source, admits uncertainty and has its possible errors and bias considered.

points.title: Repeatable and reproducible research
points.brief: A finding is stronger when the same researchers can repeat it and others can reproduce it with new participants.

units.title: Unit 2: How do internal and external factors influence behaviour and mental processes?

points.title: Person perception
points.brief: The quick judgements we form about other people from cues such as appearance, body language and what we already believe.

points.title: Attributions
points.brief: Explaining behaviour by the person (internal) or the situation (external). The fundamental attribution error leans too far toward the person when judging others.

points.title: The tri-component model of attitudes
points.brief: An attitude has three parts that can disagree with each other, affective (feelings), behavioural (actions) and cognitive (beliefs).

points.title: Stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination
points.brief: A stereotype is a belief about a group, prejudice is a negative attitude toward it, and discrimination is acting unfairly toward its members.

points.title: Cognitive dissonance
points.brief: The discomfort of holding beliefs that clash with actions. People reduce it by changing a belief, changing the action or explaining the gap away.

points.title: Heuristics in decisions
points.brief: Mental shortcuts such as availability and anchoring make decisions fast, but can lead to systematic errors.

points.title: Stigma and reducing prejudice
points.brief: Prejudice, discrimination and stigma harm wellbeing. Contact between groups on equal terms, shared goals and challenging stereotypes reduce them.

points.title: Status, power and culture
points.brief: A person's status and power in a group, and cultural norms, shape how people act toward them and how much influence they have.

points.title: Conformity and Asch
points.brief: Conformity is changing behaviour to match a group. Asch's line study found many people gave a clearly wrong answer to match others.

points.title: What affects conformity
points.brief: Group size, unanimity, deindividuation and social proof all change how likely someone is to conform. Normative and informational influence explain why.

points.title: Obedience and Milgram
points.brief: Obedience is following orders from an authority. Milgram found most people kept giving what they thought were shocks when told to.

points.title: Media and behaviour
points.brief: Media and social media can build connection, but can also feed social comparison, addictive use and harmful norms.

points.title: Independence and anti-conformity
points.brief: Knowing how groups influence us helps people think for themselves and resist pressure when a group is wrong.

points.title: Sensation and perception compared
points.brief: Sensation is detecting stimuli with sense receptors. Perception is the brain selecting, organising and interpreting that information.

points.title: Reception, transduction and transmission
points.brief: Receptors detect a stimulus, transduction turns it into electrical impulses, and transmission carries those impulses to the brain.

points.title: Attention
points.brief: Selective attention focuses on one thing, divided attention splits across tasks, and sustained attention holds focus over time.

points.title: Top-down and bottom-up processing
points.brief: Bottom-up processing builds perception from raw sensory data; top-down processing uses knowledge and expectations to interpret it.

points.title: Gestalt principles
points.brief: The brain groups visual information using principles such as figure-ground, closure, similarity and proximity.

points.title: Depth cues
points.brief: Binocular cues use both eyes, such as convergence and retinal disparity. Monocular cues work with one eye, such as linear perspective and interposition.

points.title: Perceptual set
points.brief: Expectations, context, past experience and motivation prepare us to see or taste things a certain way.

points.title: Gustatory perception
points.brief: Taste combines signals from taste receptors with smell, texture and sight. Biological, psychological and social factors all shape it.

points.title: Visual illusions
points.brief: Illusions such as the Müller-Lyer and Ames room show vision can be wrong. In agnosia, a person sees an object but cannot recognise it.

points.title: Distortions of taste
points.brief: Supertasters taste more strongly, miracle berries make sour food taste sweet, and food colour changes the flavours people report.

points.title: Synaesthesia and spatial neglect
points.brief: In synaesthesia one sense triggers another, such as seeing colours with sounds. In spatial neglect a person ignores one side of space.

points.title: Aims, hypotheses, models and theories in psychology
points.brief: An aim states what is studied, a hypothesis predicts a result, and models and theories explain what is observed.

points.title: Variables and hypotheses
points.brief: The independent variable is changed, the dependent variable is measured, and a hypothesis predicts how one affects the other in a given population.

points.title: Controlled and extraneous variables
points.brief: Extraneous variables could affect results. Controlled variables are kept the same so only the independent variable changes. A confounding variable has already affected the results.

points.title: Sampling
points.brief: A sample is drawn from a population. Random and stratified sampling help it represent the population, so results can be generalised.

points.title: Research methods
points.brief: Controlled experiments, correlational studies, case studies and fieldwork suit different questions. Experiments use within-subjects, between-subjects or mixed designs.

points.title: Ethics in research
points.brief: Psychology research must protect participants with informed consent, voluntary participation, withdrawal rights, confidentiality and debriefing, and only use deception when justified.

points.title: Data and error
points.brief: Data can be qualitative or quantitative, and primary or secondary. Random errors scatter results; systematic errors push them one way.
